doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

chapter: The future of New Orleans music
title: Jazz Fest audiences, playing true to himself and funk bands
summary: Tourists want new sounds, the Jazz Fest tent grew, he refuses to play only Saints, and chose jazz for honesty after college; funk bands taught him.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Do you think there is economic considerations there like tourists aren’t going to come to New Orleans or when they come they want to hear the traditional music, what they’re expecting?

Not really because there are a lot of tourists that come to New Orleans and have heard things like that and say man, I’ve been looking for that all day around here. I didn’t know that existed in New Orleans you know. It’s just that it hasn’t been exposed because the people who are trying to make money off you don’t think they can make enough. But like I was going to say, at the Jazz Fest when we started playing, twenty-five, thirty years ago, the tent, the jazz tent would be full from the act before us and when we would play in ten minutes that tent would be empty. The only people left would be our family members you know. But over a period of time the tent has grown and people want to hear that. Because it’s a new experience. It’s the thing that makes them look within their own minds and try to understand what’s going on. You keep hearing the same old song, I am so tired of playing some of those — I love the music but I’m tired of playing — I don’t want to play some of those same old traditional. I don’t want to play “When the Saints Go Marching In.” I love it, but there are enough other people playing it. I don’t want to do that. And I want to play my thoughts. I want to be honest about it. I want to play how I feel. Some days I feel this way and some days I don’t and that’s one of the decisions I made like coming out of college and trying to get a career in classical music or jazz and I thought about it and I said okay on a day I might not feel like playing this part I have to play in the orchestra. I’m being honest with myself. So I pursued the jazz because I could play the way I felt. If I didn’t feel like playing a high note I didn’t have to play that note. I could play according to how I felt at that moment. And I was being true to myself. And I played with a lot of funk bands which I learned a lot. Even though I was playing funk music I was on the bandstand always concentrating on playing my instrument correctly with the correct attack, the correct air, the correct sound. So I wasn’t up there that I was © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
just dancing and having a good time man, I was still learning music and I learned a lot because I was around great musicians too.
